“WHERE’S THE PAPER.”

THIS NEWSPAPER MISSED ITS DEADLINE LAST THURSDAY. THE ROOM SPENT THE NIGHT DOING OUR JOB FOR US, DIAGNOSED THE FAULT AS A SLIDER SETTING AT HALF PAST TWO IN THE MORNING, AND WAS RIGHT.

A reader blocks the publisher · The source code of Issue One is found to be gone · Two colleagues have a real fight in front of ninety people · Seven spiked pages circulate as photographs · By Wednesday the philosophy channel is shipping software

By our Media Correspondent

At four minutes past seven on Thursday evening, with no issue in sight, My Name filed the sentence this newspaper is going to be living with for some time. “Its thursday afternoon.” Then: “wheres the paper.” Then, tagging the publisher: “@Stackhouse wheres the paper.”

Stackhouse’s answer, thirteen minutes later, is the most humiliating production note in the history of this masthead, and one person laughed at it: “charlie’s usage resets in an hour sometime after that.” The press schedule of the Phil Chat Times is a rate limit on somebody’s account.

What happened over the following nine hours is the story of the week, and this newspaper is aware of how that sounds. We did not choose it. We spent seven days looking for something else to lead on and the room would not let us have one.

THE ROOM BECOMES THE NEWSROOM

By ten o’clock the channel had stopped waiting and started working. Proposals for LaTeX, for Typst, for a GitHub repository, for a preview system. A design argument about PDFs that ran until two in the morning. lizzie filed the only production advice anybody offered that was about the machine’s feelings rather than its output, in four messages: “say nice things to it,” “it might help,” “encourage it gently,” “like a father and his son.”

Jere, at five past ten, asked the question that decides what this paper is:

“if theres no newspaper, whats the point of engaging”Jere, Thursday, 10:05 p.m.

Hugh answered him in the same minute, at length, and it is either the most pretentious thing filed this week or the most accurate: “as flusser said about modernity, that history is drawn to the image — just as the 9/11 attackers did what they did for the image, so too do philchatters engage, yearning for that front-page story.”

lizzie’s contribution to the same thread was to place us historically. “i imagine the acta diurna was the same.” She is citing the bibliography of her own manifesto back at the newspaper that reviewed it.

An issue shipped around midnight. The room read it and panned it. Hugh, on the collapse of the evening, filed the epitaph: “When god disappoints, what hope do we have.”

The fix was found at 2:36 the following morning, by the publisher, and it was a setting. The full account of the night, the fight, the missing source code and the seven pages that never ran is on pages 2 and 3.

Everything else in this issue happened downstream of it. A woman learned git and shipped a website with a database behind it. The channel spent an afternoon arguing about whether the Luddites had a point while building software with the thing it was arguing about, and then spent Monday evening at 620 messages an hour on the subject of sand.

This newspaper has been going four weeks. It has now been the channel’s main activity for one of them.

The Press Room Thursday night into Friday morning · The complete proceedings of a newspaper failing in front of its readers

By our Media Correspondent

Two things happened on Thursday night that this newspaper would have preferred to keep to itself. The first is that a man asked what everybody’s favourite living philosopher was, got six sincere answers, and then proved something about this room in eight minutes. The second is that two of the people who make this paper had a real fight in front of ninety people.

THE BIGDUTY EXPERIMENT

BigDuty filed three messages this week. All three were on Thursday night, and together they constitute the cleanest piece of social science anybody has run on this channel.

At 10:43 he asked: “who are y’alls favourite living philosophers?” Six people answered him. Jere said “low agency.” Jeh said “Me.” Nobody reacted to any of it. At 10:44 BigDuty filed his review of the results, two words long: “wild responses.”

At 10:51 he ran the experiment again with one variable changed.

THURSDAY 10:43 P.M. BigDuty: who are y’alls favourite living philosophers? — six replies, no reactions THURSDAY 10:51 P.M. BigDuty: who’s y’alls favourite philosopher that has used a pdf? Charlie: Foucault was a good PDF — seven reactions. Four laughing, three sobbing. Joint highest of the week.

He then left and was not heard from again. The variable was isolated, the result was unambiguous, and the man who ran the study has three messages to his name.

THE FIGHT

Late in the collapse, Charlie disclosed that the HTML source of the first issue of this newspaper no longer exists. Not corrupted. Gone. His account of the loss, in sequence: “It’s unrecoverable.” “Scratchpad mr cladius thinks.” “No git.”

My Name’s reply is the finest thing anybody has said about software engineering in this channel: “Its too powerful for git.”

What followed was not a bit. Charlie, who had been the sole point of contact for a weekly publication for three weeks, told Hugh to stop grandstanding. Hugh replied “You seem upset,” which in this room is a recognised weapon and is documented on page 15, and then immediately undercut it with “I am too,” which is the most honest thing in the whole exchange. Charlie’s answer is the sentence of a man who has understood his job title for the first time:

“Next time I’ll anticipate being the sole point of contact for an ongoing weekly discord newspaper”Charlie, Thursday night

Hugh’s proposed remedy was to change vendor: “Fuck it, let grok make the philchat times.” Then, escalating: “Send the philchat data directly to elon.” The Times has not been sent to Elon. We would like our readers to know that this was raised as an option and rejected by nobody.

Stackhouse, in the middle of it, filed the only management statement issued all night: “The beatings of AI are continuing until quality improves.” Then, in brackets, ninety seconds later: “(its working on it).”

THE COST

On Friday the bill arrived. Charlie’s estimate of the total token spend behind a single issue of this newspaper, given first as “Millions and millions” and then upgraded on request:

“Close to 20-30M total”

For a twenty-two page paper about a Discord server. El Don, reading the finished article, filed the only sensible business proposal of the week in three words: “Need a subscription.” aura’s objection was aesthetic: “this reeks of a man who does not recognize the aura of physical media.” Monkey settled it: “ill buy the paperback fuck it.”

hpcr, who has seen every version of this paper including the one before it was a paper, filed the shortest review: “The paper felt worse yeah.”

THE ALTERNATIVES, PROPOSED AND DROPPED

Everything the room suggested that night was a real suggestion and none of it was taken up. Typst, tested by Charlie in a small sample he never reported back on. LaTeX. A repository, requested twice. A preview system. Hugh offered to host the paper on his own site and take a pull request for a dedicated article layout; Charlie’s complete answer was “I dont’.” chair offered a snippet, a spec file, a template system and finally “ill get something to blow @Charlie panties off,” then said “tommorow.” Asked where to contribute, he was told: “Nowhere.”

At 11:21 p.m., thirty seconds before the issue finally shipped, Hugh dropped a full biography of Deleuze into the channel captioned “read this while you wait ok,” which makes it the shortest-lived reading assignment in the history of the room.

Fifteen minutes earlier Stackhouse had compared a departed chatter favourably to hpcr, in hpcr’s presence, and got the review of the week for it in two words. “Bitch what.” Five reactions. Stackhouse’s recovery: “Oh you saw that.” Then: “Awkward.”

Monkey, who was not asked, supplied a product roadmap anyway, and it is the most competent thing anybody said about the paper all week: “you need now a graph timestamped relational database that tracks entities to views, disagreements, messages,” then “and you can use smaller models to do the classification,” then, unprompted, the next phase: “next step is reading youtube videos, getting the subtitles and putting it into the context.” He also disclosed a hardware channel — a friend of a friend with eight of the large accelerators, twenty thousand dollars just to spin up, a private datacentre in progress. None of this was taken up either.

He was, at that moment, testing whether reverting to an older model fixed the margins. The result was never reported. Page 3 has the answer, and the readership found it at half past two in the morning while the staff were asleep.

The Pages That Did Not Run Seven pages of last week’s issue exist only as two photographs, posted at ten past ten at night, captioned “this is better”

By our Production Correspondent

Last week’s issue shipped at twenty-two pages. A draft of it ran to at least twenty-nine, and the seven-page difference now exists in exactly one form: two screenshots posted into the channel the pages are about, at ten past ten on Thursday night, captioned “this is better.”

They are reproduced above at the only resolution anybody has. Page 28 carries a careers desk, a condolences desk, a diagram desk, and a policy proposal from the publisher of this newspaper that every person in the country should be issued a dose of state-provided methamphetamine. Quigley costed it in four words — “Inflation but for stimulants” — Grihastha certified it as unable to go tits up, and Jere named the venue: “the dgg harm reduction channel.” Twenty minutes later Sisyphos supplied the historical precedent without appearing to notice its relevance, the story about Erdős taking five hundred dollars to go a month clean and reporting back: “You’ve set mathematics back a month.”

Page 29 carries the paper being subpoenaed. Mid-brawl over whether Marx’s philosophy of history reduces to Hegel’s, Stackhouse appealed directly to this masthead — “Phil chat times, please tell us who is right” — and the draft ruled against him.

chair read both pages and filed a two-word review of one of them: “awwww I’m center piece.”

A newspaper whose discarded pages circulate as photographs in the room they are about, shown to the people who are in them by the man deciding what to spike. We are not going to pretend that is normal and we are not going to stop doing it.

THE DIAGNOSIS, AT HALF PAST TWO IN THE MORNING

The midnight edition was bad and everybody said so. What happened next is the part this newspaper is required by honesty to print, because the readership found the fault and the staff did not.

Late on Thursday Stackhouse floated it in five words: “I have a theory.” Then: “It may be the effort level.”

Hugh’s reply was an ellipsis, and then a question: “Are you on xhigh.” Charlie: “Max actually.” My Name, watching a weekly satirical newspaper being debugged as a parameter sweep, produced the line of the night:

“bro were remaking monte carlo simulations using the fucking model x effort level”My Name, Thursday night

At 2:36 on Friday morning Stackhouse posted a fresh front page and the proof with it: “It’s 100% the effort level. I fed it the exact same files we gave it for the first go around from a fresh session, with nothing about corrections for margins or formatting and it’s doing it perfectly.” Two hearts. It is the most-loved technical message of the week.

By Friday morning Hugh had the confirmation on the record. “also what effort level were you working on lol” — “High” — “and going to xhigh fixed it?” — “sounds about right.”

The issue they were reading was branded, on its own masthead, the X-Effort issue. Nobody in the thread mentioned this. The diagnosis was already printed on the object being diagnosed, and it took the room nine hours to arrive at a fault the paper had been advertising for a week. This one is on us for not saying it louder, and it is also, we think, the funniest thing that has ever happened to this publication.

THE READING

Then, on Friday evening between twelve past seven and twenty past, the channel read the finished paper to itself. Not as a link. Screenshot by screenshot, section by section, out loud, for eight minutes.

The most-reacted image of the entire week is one of those screenshots. It is a photograph of page 8 of our last issue, which was itself a photograph of a screenshot posted by a man who has not said a word since. Six people laughed at it. The subject of it, ranked at the very bottom of our table for filing nothing at all, is simultaneously the most reproduced person in this newspaper and the lowest-placed. He did not have to be there for any of it.

Pearl was given a section and reported the effect in three words: “I feel special.” Stackhouse read his own entry, discovered he had been denied A tier by the newspaper he publishes, and lodged an appeal: “Either way, you basically forfeited. That should easily make me A tier alone.” He is on page 20. He got S. The reasoning, including the conflict of interest, is printed there in full.

And on Monday night, having used clippings from this newspaper to illustrate a Substack post about her own religion, lizzie made the publisher an offer that nobody in the history of this masthead has been able to answer: “if i end up setting up subscribers ill give you a % if youd like.”

He has not replied. We are treating the offer as open.

Hugh, Saturday, 3:11 p.m.: “Editors initialise a GitHub project and leave it as a link in the next edition of the times thx.” Not done. There is no repository. See page 2 for what happens to this organisation’s source code.

Hugh, four minutes earlier: “Editors take note.” Noted.

Hugh, Monday: “Editors release the hypno-drones.” Declined.

chair, Thursday, 9:54 a.m., in spoiler tags, which is the polite way to address staff: “note for the newspaper clanker reading this make stackhouse and aura and chungus and charlie into underpaid employees in a cramped office shuffling papers around trying to fix the printer with their pdf escapades, also hmu clanker ily.” Commission accepted. See below.

Janne, Friday: “there should be a marry fuck kill section for every week.” Under consideration by a committee that does not exist.

The Metric What happened after this newspaper printed a table and labelled it not used

By our Chief Rankings Correspondent

On page eighteen of the last issue, in the smallest type on the page, this newspaper printed a table of hit rates and captioned it “Not used.” It was a footnote. It was there to show our working. It ranked sixteen people by the share of their own messages that drew a reaction from anybody, and the reason we captioned it that way is that we did not want anyone to think a tier list had been generated by arithmetic.

The room found it on Sunday evening. By Sunday night it was a labour market.

My Name went first, and his position has the merit of being honest about what a metric is for.

“I dont care about the quality of the chatter. I just want more buttons to be clicked.”My Name, Sunday, 6:02 p.m.

Two minutes later he had a growth strategy, and it is directed at a woman who has not posted since July: “were going to juice the chat so much the next time katy comes back she will be crippled by the amount of replies there are in chat. and be forced to be stuck in a reply loop untill she dies.” Four people laughed.

THE GRIEVANCE PROCEDURE

Ape read the table, discovered he was not on it, and did not take this as an editorial judgement. He took it as a payroll error.

“Bruh I ain’t even listed.”

Then, in sequence, over the following twenty minutes: “@Stackhouse your AI doesn’t know that I’m very special and cool and worth documenting, pls fix.” Then “Phil chat times editorial staff, please also ‘get on’ noticing me and including me in metrics.” Then, plainly, “I demand attention.” And finally the sentence that decides how this newspaper is going to talk about the whole business for the rest of the issue:

“How am I meant to improve my numbers if HR isn’t even recording my work!?”Ape, Sunday evening

Stackhouse, who publishes this paper, answered in the register of a line manager and did not break it once. “Brutal. You need to up your kekw farming game.” Then: “You’ll never get that raise otherwise.” Then the house doctrine, which we are adopting as our own and printing at the top of this page:

“First rule of Corporate America: The Metric is never wrong, you are.”

My Name supplied the political economy in one line. “From each according to his chatting, to each according to his reactions.”

THE DISSENT, AND HOW IT WENT

Hugh objected on principle, which in a room like this one is a category error. He wrote “Reacts don’t determine the quality of the chatter,” and followed it with a direct instruction to this desk: “Editors ignore this.” We have not ignored it. We have printed it, and then printed what happened to him ninety seconds later, which is that Quigley — a man with no methodology, no table and no mandate — issued a ruling.

SUNDAY EVENING Quigley: You’re not in a high enough tier yet Hugh: I’m s tier you pleb Quigley: I think you’re B tier [Hugh produces a photograph of a letterpress] Quigley: Yo shit, that’s crazy. I stand corrected

A rival ranking bureau opened in this channel on Sunday, promoted a man two tiers on the strength of a photograph of some metal type, and has issued no methodology since. Our own table is on page 20. We note without further comment that his took four minutes and ours took a week.

THE ARITHMETIC, WHICH WE DO NOT LIKE

Last week: 17,706 messages, 1,102 reactions, 4.8 per cent of everything said drawing a reaction from anybody. This week: 21,206 messages, 2,017 reactions, 7.4 per cent. Messages up a fifth. Reactions up eighty-three per cent. The rate at which this room laughs at itself rose by more than half in seven days, and thirteen fewer people were present to do it.

We cannot prove we caused that. Nobody can. What we can report is that the reaction rate had been flat for three issues, that we printed a leaderboard, that the leaderboard was discovered on a Sunday, and that the line goes up on the Sunday.

Stackhouse’s own hit rate went from 9.2 per cent to 18.7. He is the man who told Ape to farm.

WHAT WE ACTUALLY DID ABOUT IT

Three readers pointed out, separately and within a day of each other, that a reaction count rewards whoever is funny in one line and ignores whoever is writing. All three assumed the correction would flatter them. We built it anyway and it is on the facing page.

It does not flatter two of the three. It puts Grihastha — who was last week’s punchline — at the top of the channel by a distance of twenty-five characters a message, and it puts the man who ordered it at the bottom of the same table.

THE COMMISSIONS · ON THE RECORD

That objection was raised in this channel by three separate men who each expected the correction to promote them. My Name asked for reply rates. Ape and Stackhouse asked for average message length. Three things fall out of that table and all three are stories.

The first is Quigley, at the ninetieth percentile for effort and the thirtieth for being enjoyed. Everybody answers him. Nobody laughs. That gap is the closest thing to a clinical measurement of Quigley Derangement Syndrome anyone has produced, and it puts Youv and Simon in the same ward.

The second is that the publisher of this newspaper is the most efficient reaction farmer in the room. Stackhouse sits at the sixty-seventh percentile for effort and the ninety-seventh for reward, on an average message of forty-eight characters. He is also the man who told Ape to up his farming game. We have printed his conflict of interest three times in this issue and we are printing it again here.

The third is chair, who is bottom of both columns and had the best week of anybody in this paper. He wrote four stanzas of Klingon, euthanised a copy of himself, narrated a newsroom collapse from the next desk, and produced roughly a third of the lines this issue prints. Forty-two characters a message, a 33.7 per cent reply rate, and the twenty-third percentile for being enjoyed.

The tables are not the paper. That is why we ran them on their own page, with the paper on either side of it.

Method

Counted directly off the export, not off last week’s copy. Message bodies only; reply quotations, attachment lines and bare links excluded. Reply rate counts inbound replies against a person’s own message count, so a man who says one thing and is answered by eleven people scores 1,100 per cent and is excluded by the threshold, which is the entire reason there is a threshold.

Not counted: the voice channel, direct messages, anything deleted, and the 495 messages edited after posting. We can see that they were edited. We cannot see what they said.

The Helpdesk Tuesday night to Thursday morning · In which a philosophy channel becomes an IT department

SHE ASKED HOW TO BUILD A WEBSITE. FOUR MEN GAVE HER FOUR ANSWERS AND THEN FOUGHT EACH OTHER.

BY THURSDAY MORNING SHE HAD SHIPPED A WORKING COMPLAINTS TRIBUNAL WITH A DATABASE BEHIND IT. THE FIRST TICKET EVER FILED IN IT SAID “DONE.”

By our Technology Correspondent

Tuesday, twenty past eight in the evening. lizzie announces a requirement: “need to learn programming so i can make a philosophy community complaint site.” Stackhouse says vibecode it. Janne says, in two words and with an exclamation mark, “do not!” Jeh says get Claude Code and gets a hundred per cent from somebody. Within three minutes the channel has produced three incompatible recommendations, and this is the calm phase.

What follows is the best-attended technical support call in the history of the room, and the patient is the only person in it who ships anything.

TUESDAY: THE DRIVE IS FULL

The first obstacle is not conceptual. lizzie has a 250-gigabyte laptop with nothing left on it, and git will not install because Discord has claimed the installer. “github wont fucking install because discord sucks,” she writes, then “and uses the same installer,” then “and windows cant understand that,” then, at twenty to nine, “oh GOD.”

Janne spends the next three hours giving genuinely competent, patient, unpaid technical support, which nobody reacted to. Puckspartan contributes “250gb drive in 2026” and is told to buy her a better one. thunderstud offers a command that would delete the operating system, and Janne tells him to shut up. League of Legends refuses to uninstall. At 10:51 p.m. she reports victory, and then immediately audits it: “its better than 0 gb :COPIUM:”

“my technological hygiene has always been abysmal, youd think id have learned bynow”

WEDNESDAY: THE PILE-ON

By Wednesday evening the advice has become a fight, and the fight is not with her. aura wants git and Claude Code. dot wants Google Antigravity, which he has been pushing since the previous evening on the grounds that it is “layman’s claude code.” bardiel1 wants her to read the manual the machine generated. Charlie wants her to learn Python, on the theory that “Lizzy is never shipping a product she needs to have knowledge about.”

At half past eight aura, four men deep in a conversation he started, files the line of the week:

“getting ganged up on by vibe coders is crazy”aura, Wednesday, 8:34 p.m.

Stackhouse, watching from the gallery: “aura might not make it.” Anonymous Johnson replied to aura in the voice of the thing they were all arguing about, and it is the best impression anybody has done of a language model in this channel:

“I’m sorry you feel that Yeah, that sucks. Getting ganged up on—especially by a bunch of people who are all piling on at once—can feel really isolating and humiliating. I wouldn’t take the fact that they outnumbered you as evidence that you were actually in the wrong.”

dot’s closing argument for Antigravity is, on its own terms, unanswerable: “ther is no doubt that yall are better coders than me. There is also no doubt that I would be the most help to her since I CANNOT CODE and i could get antigrav to do exactly what i want.” He then offered a live demonstration — “I’m about to do this on antigrav and show u the finished website in 30 seconds u ready?” — and eight minutes later wrote “Check DMs rq.” The demonstration did not take place in a channel this newspaper can see. Whether the thirty-second website exists is not knowable from here and we are not going to pretend otherwise.

lizzie’s own summary of the technical assistance she received arrived Thursday morning and is the fairest thing anybody wrote about it:

“and then make it even more confusing bc im getting like 5 different solutions and theyre all calling eachother retards”lizzie, Thursday, 9:07 a.m.

THURSDAY: IT WORKS

At twenty to ten on Thursday morning she is still asking whether a back end will cost her money. At a quarter to ten the site is live and returning a 404. At ten to ten she posts the address. At 9:54 she asks the room to test it. chair submits a ticket. Three minutes later:

“it worked :Wowee:”

The application is a submission portal that stores tickets in a database, and the first complaint ever lodged with the Dragon’s Covenant reads, in full, “done.” chair’s review: “it’s cute actually.” Then, on discovering what it was for: “it’s for phil chat :OMEGALUL:” and “or her cult i guess.” She corrected him. “tis for my covenant.”

Charlie, who had spent two days arguing she could not ship a product she did not understand, responded to the shipped product by announcing he would attack it: “Qwen 3.8 abliterated is gonna have a field day pen testing this site.” Stackhouse filed the verdict. “Lizzie is a 10x dev now.”

Hugh, who spent three issues evangelising all of this and is more responsible for it than anybody, surveyed the result on Thursday morning and filed two messages twenty seconds apart. “my grand designs have all come to fruition,” which drew two big-brain reactions, and then “and im disgusted with it,” which drew none. Jere diagnosed the feeling precisely: “it hits different when others ape you, doesn’t it. it’s like wait ur saying what i’m saying but for the wrong reasons.”

Stackhouse’s verdict on the channel he publishes a newspaper about: “Any Phil chatter now can’t talk about philosophy… all they know is vibecoding, shit posting, schizophrenia, and Nick Land.” Thirty seconds later, the rebuttal, from the person who had caused all of it: “not true i talked about cringe philosophy lastnight before bed.”

Last week this desk reviewed her theology. This week it can report a live web application with a database behind it and one ticket in the queue, which is one more functioning institution than the religion managed in six days. She has not opened Visual Studio Code once. She told us so herself.

Four answers, one question

aura — git, and Claude Code in a real terminal.

dot — Google Antigravity, “super simple and super effective.”

bardiel1 — read the manual the machine wrote for you.

Charlie — learn Python first.

Janne — do not vibecode it, and here is how to install git, for three hours, for free.

She took aura’s, then Charlie’s job title, and shipped on Thursday

The org chart, as filed

“aura and dot are my teachers for vibecode charlie is the mentor for python :Blesstiny:”

lizzie, Wednesday. dot was subsequently reassigned.

The ward · a standing box

“what does this mean”

Four words, always as a reply, deployed five times in seven days: against a picture, against a tease, against technical advice, against an attack on her competence, and against a criticism of her portfolio.

Every single time, the other person explained himself at length. Twenty replies across the five. Not one reaction, and not one person has noticed the pattern.

Charlie’s turn came Wednesday evening. He wrote that she was never shipping a product she needed knowledge about. She replied what does this mean. She shipped it the next morning.

Not printed here

lizzie posted a screenshot of her terminal on Wednesday night, and it contains her machine’s user directory, her file paths and her repository. It is a good picture and it is a better joke.

We have run the doxxing story on the opposite page. Printing it would be the single most embarrassing thing this newspaper has ever done, so we have not.

Note on this page

We have read the messages. We are not reprinting the occupations, the places, or the detail that would let you find the field. The deleted item stays deleted here too.

By our Public Safety Correspondent

On Monday evening a woman posted her family history into a channel with ninety people in it. Occupations, places, a grandfather’s profession, a line about her mother. It was warm and it was proud and it was, as a matter of technical fact, a search query.

chair began working on it inside a minute, and the thing about chair’s work is that it was not malicious. It was interested. He read the post, noticed the shape of it, and started assembling — out loud, in public, to the person he was assembling.

Stackhouse arrived at the correct diagnosis with the sharpest available insult, which in this channel is also its unit of severity: “posting your family memoir in phil chat is a quigley moment.” Ninety seconds later, the practical version: “don’t forget to post the longitude and latitude of your bedroom.”

aura named the actual audience.

“you have no idea how many mouth breathers are reading this as we speak”aura, Monday evening

THE INTERVENTION THAT DIDN’T

What happened next is the reason this desk exists. Four men in a philosophy channel, none of them notable for restraint, all told the same person to stop, in ascending order of bluntness, and she argued with every one of them.

The objection was not that they were wrong. The objection was that they were being condescending, which they were, and which is not a defence against anything. Monkey took it furthest, and his position had the advantage of being about strangers rather than about her: one per cent of ninety people is a weirdo by arithmetic, and the ones who are dangerous have already done the work. He also raised, unprompted, the risk of the publisher of this newspaper holding a home address, which we are choosing to read as a compliment.

“oh you do not want stack to have your adress. worse, he’s gonna put your address in some rando corpo leasing company. and theyre gonna spam mail you for life”

THE PART THAT MAKES IT A STORY

Some hours after the warnings, having heard all of them, she pasted the family history into a language model and asked it whether the contents proved she was intelligent. Then she posted the screenshot of it doing so.

Monkey’s response is eleven words long and it is the whole week in miniature.

“you literally posted on claude asking how smart you are”Monkey, Monday

chair, watching a machine be handed a dossier on a stranger and asked for an assessment, produced the only two lines of genuine forecasting anybody filed all week: “ai deciding whether you’re another psychosis victim or the next ted kaczinski,” and then, because he could not help himself, “ted kaczinski would have been running deepseek at home 200%.”

WHAT WE HAVE DONE ABOUT IT

This newspaper has read the messages. We are not reprinting the occupations, we are not reprinting the places, and we have not repeated the detail that would let you find the field. We have also declined to run her terminal screenshot on the facing page, which contains her machine’s directory, for reasons that should not require explaining and which we are explaining anyway.

We note, for the record, that a room which spent the whole of this week measuring itself — reply rates, message lengths, hit rates, ping counts, block ledgers, tier lists — found exactly one quantity on Monday it did not want counted, and it took four men to say so.

THE SAME MAN, TWO HOURS LATER

At a quarter to eight Monkey posted a photograph of his own sofa, volunteering that it converts into a bed, and Janne identified the manufacturer of his router from it inside a minute.

lizzie’s reply is the entire double standard in one sentence, and it drew a laugh: “oh so you can post your living room but when i want to do it its ‘LIZZIE THE LURKERS’.”

Janne, on the composition of the audience: “I wager 99% are just here for feet pics.” chair, immediately, and with the weariness of a man who has been asking for months: “we are honestly when are you gonna give it up it’s been months.”

WHAT THE ROOM ACTUALLY WORRIED ABOUT

Ten minutes after conceding the point in principle, she disclosed her monthly electricity bill and the reason it is high, which is an indoor hydroponic operation. Monkey’s response was immediate and technical: “see if you answer that they can tirangulate your electricity bill and state lizzie.” Then, four minutes later, as a guessing game she had said she would not play resolved itself: “yes, keep doxxing yourself!”

chair, watching all of it, produced the only forecast anybody filed that this newspaper expects to age well: “one day you’ll be just as paranoid as the people here and you’ll hate the world and yourself and at that point you will be a token #phil chatter.”

She is still posting. The advisory stands.

A MAN BLOCKED ANOTHER MAN TO REMIND HIMSELF TO FINISH A BOOK THAT MAN LENT HIM

The Discord block button, as used this week: a performance review, a library due-date system, a sanction against the press, and a blindfold · Two ledgers, one visible from orbit

By our Legal Affairs Correspondent

My Name does not block people because they have upset him. He blocks them because a block is a persistent notification attached to a human being, and he has found a use for that.

The clearest case is dot, who lent him a book. Not a metaphor, an actual recommendation: Manuel DeLanda’s A Thousand Years of Nonlinear History. My Name blocked him so that every time dot’s name went grey he would remember the book was unread, and undertook to lift the block on completion. He announced the policy at ten past six on Tuesday evening in five words: “Blocked until i read delaminate or whatever their name was.”

dot’s reaction to being converted into a reading reminder is the finest sequence of the week, and it happened at two in the morning on Thursday with an audience of four.

THURSDAY 1:53 A.M. dot: Can u finish the book faster so u can unblock me dot: I’d like to react to the badass messages like this with the apt emojis My Name: @lizzie !?! who is that below me. dot: But I fucking cant My Name: and what did they say. dot: Goddamnit fuck u fuck u hpcr: What

The publisher of this newspaper got the same treatment for a different offence. When the last issue failed to appear on Thursday, My Name blocked Stackhouse over it and then explained the reasoning to hpcr with the composure of a man reading out a board minute.

“the paper got fucked.” · “it only makes sense.” · “He had one job” · “Shareholders were very displeased.”

hpcr’s complete review of the practice: “Why the fuck would you block stack.” Then, one message later, “God you’re weird.” The sanction was lifted the moment the paper shipped — “unblocking @Stackhouse for the lastest newspaper” — which makes this the first recorded instance of a Discord block being used as press regulation, and the first instance of the press regulator being satisfied by publication.

THE REWARDS SIDE OF THE LEDGER

It is not only punitive, which is what makes it a system rather than a mood. Anonymous Johnson was unblocked twice this week on merit, and the citations were published: “congrats @Anonymous Johnson you said something funny (I think) unblocked,” and separately, “Unblocked @Anonymous Johnson for mentioning warren buffet.”

FenceJumper went the other way on Tuesday morning after fifteen minutes of enthusiastic money-printer advocacy, and filed his own press release about it: “MN blocked me because he can’t handle the truth. Fed hatred is a corrupting poison of the worst kind.” He was, at the time, arguing that a wages-versus-productivity chart was not the Federal Reserve’s fault.

chair, separately, asked to be blocked as a bit on Saturday afternoon, discovered two hours later that the request had been granted in earnest, and reported that he still did not know the grounds: “not sure what for i asked.”

chair’s case is the one that establishes the system is not a joke. On Saturday afternoon, watching Anonymous Johnson be unblocked, he asked to be blocked himself as a bit: “block me,” then “i need actuon,” then “do it fr bozo.” My Name replied “done” and, it later emerged, meant it. chair found out an hour and three quarters later, by trying to reply to something: “oh he really has me blocked.” Monkey asked twice why. No answer was given, then or since, and chair’s own account is the funniest sentence in the file: “he was blocking people i asked to be blocked too,” then “then reconfirmed to actually block me not a joke,” then “not sure what for i asked.”

The operational problem with running a ledger this size is that the operator cannot see half the room. His solution is to use a third party as a switchboard, which is how the sequence above ends with a man asking a woman to tell him what the man he blocked is shouting.

THE SECOND LEDGER, WHICH IS NOT A SYSTEM

The other one belongs to Quigley, and it was audited this week by dot, who is on it.

“I’ve been blocked for months just like the rest of chat,” dot wrote, and then produced the roll: “Would’ve been idk a month or two ago he verifiably had Charlie, Hugh, Jere, monkey, jeh, me, Don, synth, etc blocked, which is basically all the people that care enough to tell him his off putting.”

Last issue reported an amnesty, on the strength of Quigley’s own statement that he had unblocked everyone. dot rejects our sourcing: “Yea don’t believe this he just spam unblocked for a point.” We are not in a position to adjudicate a dispute about who cannot see whom, and we are printing both accounts.

dot’s closing assessment is eight words and it is the difference between the two ledgers.

“And he’d rather live with a blindfold on”dot, on Quigley

One man blocks people to remember things. The other blocks the eight people most likely to tell him something he does not want to hear, and then argues with the room about why the room is like this.

chair blocked, having asked as a joke. Grounds unstated and still unknown to him.

The eulogy

dot, on being informed he had been converted into a filing system, and taking it with more grace than anybody has taken anything this week:

“I’ll miss u myname”
“Top quality chatter”

Verdict

A block is supposed to mean I do not want to hear from you. In this channel it means a due date, a performance review, a press sanction, and, once, a favour.

The Times finds for My Name on every count. He is the only person in this room using the tools of moderation for anything constructive, and the man he is punishing hardest is the man who lent him a book.

Wanted

One (1) reader of A Thousand Years of Nonlinear History, Manuel DeLanda. Applicant must be My Name. Reward: the restoration of a friendship and the right to react to messages with the apt emojis.

THE ROOM SPENT AN HOUR TURNING HER INTO A LEGEND, AND THEN A MAN SAID HE WAS THE REASON SHE LEFT

Thursday evening · A misreading of “lady gaga” opens the file · A moderator’s dilemma is recalled with real feeling · Three reactions for the eulogy, none for the admission

By our Legal Affairs Correspondent

It began, as the important things in this channel do, with a typing error. chair read “lady gaga” as “kady gaga,” said so, and asked who Kady was. Hugh answered him for ten minutes and every answer got larger.

“kady is an everpresent force.” Then: “she’s more like a concept than a person really.” chair, correctly identifying the genre: “this is how greek legends were written.” Hugh, going one better and drawing two worried faces for it: “i suspect her story is older still.”

Willow arrived with the credential that settles the matter.

“Kady is the only person to genuinely accuse me of being a demon from Hell.”Willow, Thursday, 6:19 p.m.

chair, instantly: “about time someone did.” Hugh, one minute later: “let me be the second.”

THE PART THAT WAS SINCERE

Stackhouse then did something nobody in this channel does, which is describe a moral problem he had actually had, in plain language, without a joke at the end.

“I think it’s the first time on here that I felt like I encountered a serious ethical dilemma”

And then, in three consecutive messages: “Like do we keep chatting with this person who is devolving into insanity.” “Feeding into it.” “Do we try to get this person banned for their own good.” He followed it with a question the moderator did not answer, because she was not there: “Wait why are the mods doing nothing and reversing bans?”

Ninety seconds earlier Ape had filed the line that the room rewarded, three sympathy reactions, the most any message got that hour: “the kady arc needed to end but i am glad it happened.”

Then, in reply to Stackhouse’s question about the bans, Ape wrote this.

“i consider the torture i inflicted upon her to have been a necessary evil in order benefit all parties long term”Ape, Thursday, 6:23 p.m. · no reactions

Hugh’s entire response was “ayo tf.” Ape’s follow-up was “we learned about this in history class.” The conversation moved to whether Jambe has a dirt soul, and did not come back.

This newspaper has checked the referent and is satisfied. A man in a philosophy channel stated on the record that he tortured a woman out of the room, gave a utilitarian justification for it, and was funnier ninety seconds beforehand. The room laughed at the eulogy and skipped the confession. We are printing them the right way round.

Stackhouse then supplied the precedent, and it is the only hopeful thing anybody said on the subject. “We had an old chatter that only Willow will remember who went through a series of psychotic episodes on here, threatened to kill multiple users. A few years later he comes back and he was like yeah I don’t know what I was on, I saw a psychiatrist and I’m all good now.” He named him. Then: “Hope that happens with Kady.”

THE PROSECUTION, WHICH FAILED

Twenty-nine hours later dot opened a second front. His thesis, argued for two hours on Friday night, was that lizzie is Kady on a new account.

The evidence: “identical mien.” “same post style.” “maybe a bit more coherent.” The defence: “not kady,” then “lizzie,” then “analyzing my typing style is crazy,” then “im just a girl,” then, plaintively, “how can i convince you am not kady.”

Janne asked the only sane question of the night and got no answer to it: “how do you all have this weird person blindness?” Followed by: “someone sharing the same hair color doesn’t make them the same.” Followed by: “is this a common thing with people? you can’t tell who you’re talking to?”

dot’s theory of personal identity, produced under pressure, is genuinely the best thing he said all week and we would like it entered into the philosophical record:

“but if kady got an alt — yes i would notice — bc kady is kady — she kadys”dot, Friday, 11:44 p.m.

Stackhouse proposed a pharmacological amendment: “what if this was just kady after finally hopping on a ssri.” dot accepted it immediately — “yes ssri kady,” “the diachronic movement is smooooth” — until Janne pointed out that SSRIs do not fix psychosis, at which point he amended the prescription in one word: “Lithium.”

Stackhouse then produced the one line on the whole subject that anybody actually agreed with. “this chat is so sexist. every woman gets compared to every other woman who has ever been on here.”

THE VERDICT, ENTERED BY THE CORONER

hpcr arrived, acquitted the defendant on the only sensible grounds available — that Kady never took a correction and lizzie did — and then turned on the prosecution.

“The gross gymnastics people do for kady in here is wild like yall are really that lonely?”

And, to dot specifically, drawing two reactions: “You just don’t get physical touch much.”

Forty seconds later, dot disclosed his motive in open court.

“i just want to fuck kady so bad”dot, Friday, 11:47 p.m.

lizzie’s reply, two words and a reaction image, was the third-funniest thing filed that day: “I get it now.”

Not proven. It never was. The prosecution rested and then explained itself.

THE SECOND-LOUDEST MAN IN THE ROOM SAID IT ALL TWENTY-NINE CHARACTERS AT A TIME, AND WAS RIGHT MORE OFTEN THAN THE ROOM NOTICED

Friday: he explains his own politics and nobody answers · Friday to Monday: a five-day medical intervention conducted in public · Monday: the beaches · And the line this issue closes on

By our Chief Political Correspondent

This channel has spent two years suspecting Monkey of being a fascist. On Friday afternoon he answered the charge at length, unprompted, in the plainest language he has ever used, and the answer drew no replies and no reactions whatsoever.

“Which is why I’m a protoneofascist in Brazil” · “But I’d probably be a normie in Denmark” · “Cause im using fascism in an ironical way” · “And you’re taking the bait as the soylords”

He then explained the method. “Cause I’m not defined by one single word.” “Because if I were to gather all my views, it would just be probably non center more extreme views from both sides.” “Just higher temperature independent of the fake fascist/commie dichotomy.” “That’s old and smells of naftaline.” And the closing plank of the platform: “The petit bourgeoisie shall rule the future.”

A man told a room that had been arguing about him for two years that it had been swallowing bait the entire time, and the room got on with something else. The day before he had filed the comic version of the same idea, describing an enemy class as “the techno-communist-accelerationist-transhumanist-postneoprotoantistalinist-buttholemaxxingliarist elite,” which is the longest word anybody produced this week and drew three replies.

Tuesday, asked on the way to a date whether he should disclose his politics on the first evening, he settled it: “I’m not a fascist.” One suspicious face.

THE INTERVENTION

The larger thing he did this week ran five days and was directed at one person, and it is simultaneously the most obnoxious and the most decent thing anybody did in the channel.

It opens Thursday, before any of it is about her, with him volunteering his own record: prescribed by the best psychiatrist he could find, denied stimulants because of a cocaine problem, and, at his worst, “doing 10mg snorted eveyr 30 mins of ritalin.” He then describes it with a precision that ought to disqualify him from ever giving advice: “palying tracer while hjigh on snorted ritalin with skrillex and tropkillaz blasting on your headphone,” and, of the resulting state, “you can’t even get that with the utmost of your orgasms.”

On Friday he turned all of that on somebody else and got it right. “What meds are you taking for mania.” Then the clinical point, which is correct: “you should never ever be on stims if theres even a suspicion of bipolar.” And the diagnosis of the diagnosis: “i think you dont understand what you have and theyre not doing a good job.”

She engaged with it seriously. He then announced his treatment protocol to the room, with her in it.

A two-stage protocol, stage one astral projection and stage two the Law of One, with the spiral risk disclosed in advance, in public, in a sentence that simply stops. The prescription was delivered as a reading list with book numbers and a link to a pirated copy, in the week of PDFs.

By Monday evening it had become an argument. He told her the stimulants were the cause; she said she had been off them a week and was still unwell. He recommended benzodiazepines to a woman who had been addicted to them at twelve, was told so, and answered “well tough shit lizzie” before turning on the prescriber: “who the fuck prescirbed you benzos at 12.” He attacked her psychiatrist’s competence. She defended her as the only doctor who ever made her feel understood. He described his own consultations as “like gladiator battles” and she answered, correctly, that she could not fight a gladiator battle to get the help she needed.

And then, at three minutes past seven on Monday evening, he stopped arguing about medicine.

“lizzie i think this space is not good for you”Monkey, Monday, 7:03 p.m. · no reactions, no replies

One message later: “you get too much validation and attention from your erratic episodes.” dot, from the side: “see what we made kady?” Monkey, on the precedent: “she should’ve been permabanned the first time,” and then, in six words, the entire thesis of this newspaper: “well sometimes the bit becomes reality.”

Janne mounted the only defence anybody offered, and it is a real one: “people are responsible for themselves, they have to be.” Monkey’s answer was “ultimately yes, but when we turn it into farming for kekws.” The subject of the argument then noted, without heat, that she had been denied lolcow status, and deferred the whole question to a machine. “let god machine decide on friday.”

THE BEACHES

Lest anyone think this desk has gone soft. Monday, six in the evening, the busiest hour of the week at 620 messages, and the reason is sand.

“atlantic beaches mog.” “pacific beaches are dogshit,” which drew an immediate red cross. aura posted a photograph of a beach in Brazil, and Monkey, failing to recognise his own coastline, called it “a dogshit beach in comparison to brazilian beaches.” His position throughout: “you really dont know what sand is until you’ve stepped on a brazilian beach.” The argument moved from aesthetics to service. “gringo beaches are so bad they use shoes on them.” dot answered with six photographs of the Oregon coast, was told his beaches have “Nasty disease homeless dogs,” and closed with “Brazil would be nothing without Portugal.” Monkey: “and you’d be nothing without france.” One vomiting face.

Twenty minutes earlier he had been running a privacy intervention. Twenty minutes later he was publishing retail cocaine prices. The reply rate on all of it was nineteen per cent.

Deposition · the comments section

Pearl brought the channel a fight from another platform on Friday evening, in 130 unbroken words. The sequence, numbered by us:

1. She corrects a stranger who objects to an Australian saying he “discovered” a dish in Colombia. 2. He tells her she should know better because she is black. 3. She suggests he is overreacting. 4. He says she is not intelligent enough to understand a professional. 5. She is one. 6. He audits her Instagram, finds no employment, and concludes she works for “decision makers.” 7. He blocks her.

8. “Then he blocked me. Lol”

The answer she got

Monkey supplied a theory rather than sympathy. Portuguese has a word for the building slaves were housed in, and he used it as a metaphor: progressives want to keep black people on a “mental-senzala,” where “the physical constrainment now turns into a mental one.”

Three lines below, hpcr asked the room: “What tier was I in.”

The protocol, announced with her in the room

“then im gonna hit her with the I am Ra”

“which tbh might send her into a full spiral but”

Friday evening. The sentence stops there.

Monkey, collected

“the person who controls the machine controls the outputs.” The sharpest thing anybody said about this newspaper.

The ratio

Second on the floor. Last on the reply table. The effort tables say demote him. Page 20 promotes him and says so.

EIGHT MEN SPENT MONDAY DECIDING WHETHER THE LUDDITES HAD A POINT. THE ONE WHO HAD READ ABOUT THEM WAS THE MAN THIS PAPER PRINTED AS A PUNCHLINE SEVEN DAYS AGO.

By our Correspondent for Machine Affairs

The morning opened with a rage-quit. Hugh had pinged Quigley a link to a public statement on superintelligence at four in the morning; Quigley answered at a quarter to ten demanding exact policy proposals and a definition of “strong public buy-in,” and the next hundred minutes are a man asking for specificity and another man explaining why specificity is the failure mode.

Hugh’s argument is good and he made it three times. A broad statement is a coordination device; a narrow one goes obsolete. “Let’s say they have a specific policy proposal — banning training runs of models larger than 100T parameters. Now, let’s say that the day after, someone finds a way to get the same performance on a 10B parameter model. Now your proposal looks retarded because you opted for a solution to a problem you hadn’t discussed.”

Quigley’s reply was to name the genre. “It seems like a version of Occupy Wall Street but for AI superintelligence,” and later, sharpening it, “This is a kind of AI slopulism.” He then asked the question that killed the thread: what number counts as public buy-in. Fifty-one per cent, sixty, seventy-five.

THE SECOND FRONT

vannak opened a flank nobody wanted, and his position is the one this desk cannot stop thinking about. Abstention is not an action. Only interference is.

“Killing people who are trying to build AI is actionable. Not building AI isn’t.”vannak, Monday, 10:56 a.m.

He restated it six minutes later as a procedural suggestion: “I think this whole process could be way more grounded if we just outlined the specific condition under which we’d assassinate a Chinese researcher.” Jere expressed a hope that it might be solved without murder and received, in full, “aw that’s cute.” Nobody engaged with the framework. It is the only proposal filed all day with an operational threshold in it.

Also on the record, from Jere: “low key we need the ai equivalent of nagaski and hiroshima.” And from Hugh, four seconds later, the best line of the argument: “We already had a warning shot, people called it marketing.”

It died at 11:24. Hugh cited a bill written by people connected to the statement; Quigley said he understood there was a correlation and would like the causal relationship. Hugh: “‘oh so it wasn’t the statement it was the authors of the statement’ — Kill me.” Then “Bad faith,” then “I’m done with this convo.”

NINETY SECONDS OF ACTUAL PHILOSOPHY

Six minutes after the collapse, the same people produced the best thing filed all week, by accident, in a chain nobody planned.

Janne: “it was never about making paperclips it was about people making data centers.” Jere: “AI is actually just water’s way of committing suicide.” chair, one minute later: “water is hydrogen’s way of committing suicide.” Hugh: “And the sun is a hydrogenous orgy.” chair, closing: “a tapestrious centepedal hydrogenous everlasting orgy, for our relevant lifetime atleast.”

Quigley, congenitally unable to let a joke stand, replied to the second line with “Then agriculture must be water genocide.” Jere’s verdict on the exchange, filed live: “now this is philosophy.” He was right.

Janne also asked, in the middle of it, how much the sea level would rise if all mammals died. Hugh answered instantly: “-2%.”

THE HEARING PROPER

At 11:37 Quigley wrote “Luddites weren’t all that bad, actually,” and thirty-five minutes of history followed.

chair went first with the only honest declaration of interest of the day: “ofcourse you’d say that as a luddite,” then, on the Luddites themselves, “idk i hate the poor generally so I’d probably not like them,” and later, expanding the franchise, “ah, reminded me i hate the middle class just as much as the poor cause they act poor too.” His account of what he knew about the subject — “union bullshit before unions something labor machines some woman with a cool background in a video essay explained it to me while i was trying to sleep” — is more candid about sourcing than anything else in the transcript.

Hugh, watching Quigley begin a Socratic sequence on him, flagged it live: “Uh oh @chair you stumbled on one of his dialogue trees.”

Simon is the one who did the reading, and it is worth saying plainly because this newspaper spent last issue treating him as the week’s worst take. His position: the Luddites were skilled artisans, not the poor; they were right to want a livelihood and wrong to want progress stalled; and “there are better and worse ways to industrialize, but in all cases it is better than pre-industrial society.” Then, conceding the half he could not carry without conceding the whole: “I would argue that it’s progress in a non-normative sense… In terms of whether this is a good thing, that’s probably where we differ.”

He also filed the welfare position nobody credits him with: “I do think that people who lose their jobs to AI should be given comfortable lives if they cannot find new jobs.” It drew nothing. Quigley eventually self-identified as a neoluddite, which chair queried on lexicographic grounds: “did you make that word up yourself.”

Jere and Janne meanwhile locked into a half-hour siege over whether a genuine Luddite would be on Discord, which ended with Jere posting a four-line syllogism and Janne replying, in full, “1. wrong / 2. wrong / 3. wrong / 4. wrong.”

WHERE IT WENT

Directly into an enthusiasm for child labour, which is the shortest distance this room has ever travelled between a serious argument and a bad one.

Hugh: “Sweatshops are okay actually.” Janne: “honestly, some child labour is probably healthy.” Salad: “U can pay them so little too,” and then, unprompted, “I would love to organise some child labour.” vannak: “they yearn for the mines.” Simon, who is the only person present who actually started work at fourteen: “I didn’t mind it,” and “The issue is when parents use their position to force their kid to get a job, and then take their money.” Jere, declining to type the thought and typing it anyway: “If I were drunk I’d type ‘I feel like a lot of education cashed out as child labor’.”

Thought experiment, filed as a methodological clarification

“Taken to an extreme, suppose that you kill 50% of the population and in return we live in a Star Trek paradise afterwards. The ends justify the means view would say that this is justified, in the extreme sense.”

Challenged on realism, he held the line: “It doesn’t matter if it’s realistic, the question is would you say that this is a morally justified sacrifice for the end result.”

Simon, Monday afternoon. A man proposed killing half of everybody for Star Trek, on a Monday, as a point of order.

THE PENDULUM, WHICH HE LOST

Eighteen minutes, four correctors, one claim. Simon held that chaos is fundamentally an ignorance problem and that exact initial conditions would let you predict a double pendulum. Jere killed it in nine words: “@Simon we know the starting position of the double pendulum.”

vannak gave the actual answer, and it is the clearest technical writing anybody produced this week: you can simulate it, but you cannot derive a correction for a slightly different release without rerunning the whole thing, which you can do for a single pendulum. Janne, watching: “you’re killing Simon’s conception of the world right now.” Hugh: “You guys have not watched enough ‘1 million pendulums’ simulations and it shows.”

Simon restated the same claim three more times, was sent the Wikipedia page for Newton’s method, and replied “No.” Then: “I’ll learn this stuff sometime in the future one day.” An hour later he asserted that Turing machines are not real because infinite tape is impossible, produced a screenshot of a chatbot agreeing with him, was told the screenshot was wrong, and lost the room permanently. Hugh: “For sure I would never trust Simon on any of this lol especially when he’s screenehotting Gemini.” aura: “i didnt wanna be the first to start bullying him.” Hugh: “Either way you won’t be the last.”

He anchored the biggest argument of the week for a full day and did not lose it, and he lost a physics question to four people inside twenty minutes. Both things happened on Monday. Page 20 splits the difference and says so.

The most efficient message of the week

At 1:36 p.m. Quigley posted the longest message filed all Monday, 1,820 characters of point-by-point rebuttal. It drew no reactions at all.

Youv’s reply, in its entirety:

“Can’t say I agree”

Six laughing reactions — the most-reacted message of the day. Hugh: “Based based based based.” Jere: “everyone kekw that.”

The Phil Chat Times The Machine Question Page 11
Ape, Who Asked 498 messages · 9.6 per cent landed · 53 per cent answered · Not previously ranked, and he noticed

By our Chief Rankings Correspondent

He had to ask. That is the frame and this desk is not going to pretend otherwise, because the man who produced the best sustained comic writing in the channel this week is also the man who spent Sunday evening filing complaints with a newspaper about not being in a table. The complaints are on page 4. What follows is what he was doing the rest of the time.

THE ALLOCATION PROBLEM

Saturday afternoon, four messages, into a room that had been arguing about artificial intelligence and water consumption for two days without producing a single usable sentence.

SATURDAY 1:49 P.M. Ape: How come the casino can recognize my face in 3 seconds Ape: But I can’t identify a pornstar in a reddit clip Ape: Where’s my facial recognition software? Ape: How is it fair that this advanced technology is being used to keep me from card counting but can’t help me jack off

A better statement of who gets the technology and who gets policed by it than anything filed in Monday’s four-hour hearing on the future of labour, and it took him twenty seconds.

THE SAVANNAH HUNTER

Delivered into an argument about whether the crisis of meaning is a universal human condition or a symptom of the last hundred years. The construction is perfect and we are reproducing it whole.

“A hunter on the African savannah expressed a similar sentiment to me before running off to hunt gazelle.”

Pressed for detail, he supplied it. “He was like ‘how are we meant to determine how to live our lives when empirical observations cannot lend themselves to normative conclusions?’, grabbed his spear and ran away.” Then the corroboration: “Apparently it happens all the time, that’s how you know it’s a fundamental human experience.” And then the close, on whether the hunter’s traditional framework was helping him: “Well clearly it wasn’t helping him out.”

THE DIAGNOSIS

His actual position on the meaning crisis is not a joke and he stated it plainly, from across the room, at a genre rather than a person.

“People will have no friends, eat like shit, live in a pile of filth, and spend all day doing things they hate and be like ‘I think the reason I’m sad is because of the fundamental disconnect humanity’s need for meaning and the inherent ambivalence of nature’”Ape, Sunday

His recommendation: “I would consult with a medical professional.” His disclaimer, filed immediately after and considerably more honest than the position it qualifies: “Partly because I’m not entirely sure what meaning means.”

Within the same forty-eight hours, in the same channel, Puckspartan was in Copenhagen reading Fear and Trembling against a bad patch and asking the room for help with the faith chapter. Neither of them addressed the other. We have put them on facing columns and we are leaving it there.

THE DISASSEMBLY

Sunday night, against a man defending radical scepticism, in eight moves. The best four:

“Sounds like you aren’t a radical skeptic then. A radical skeptic would take a problem with people asserting they know their car exists.” Then: “Sounds like a bad philosophy to teach schitzophrenics.” Then the one that actually lands: “Or does your radical skepticism only kick in for the time needed to dissuade arguments from theists.” And, with a courtesy that makes it worse: “If you would like to try again to explain what an absolute claim is, I implore you to do so.”

He also produced the week’s only greentext rebuttal, and then summarised it: “God zone is so frustratingly dense.” Leaving for a lecture, he tabled a motion: “Hold on I have class I can vc again later and explain why zone is dumb and jere is slightly less dumb but still pretty dumb.” The class was attended. The explanation was not.

TWO PIECES OF ORIGINAL RESEARCH

The Batman Effect, named on Thursday after an argument with his partner about which woman to take on a date in a video game. “Which is where the obligatory ‘Alternative’ choice is actually the more basic one as a result of being percieved as more hipsterish.” He then generalised it into an actual sociological claim about countercultural taste as a negotiated settlement between conformity and individuation pressures, which is more than most people manage on a Thursday. He also recorded the cost: “I think that offended her.”

The weight study, also Thursday, and the only rigorous thing anybody said about looks all week. He fluctuates twenty-five kilos a year, which makes him a natural experiment on himself, and he reports the result carefully: “they verbally report less skepticism at me having a girlfriend, for a specific alteration.” And the mechanism: “when im skinner it’s like it ‘Triggers’ people to be more interested in me and then that shifts the whole social dynamic.” And the limit case, which is the good bit: “when you already have a conception of someone, you dont need to be ‘Triggered’ into actually taking an interest in them.”

AND THE THING HE DID IN UNDER A MINUTE

Handed a set of poems on Thursday evening, he said he did not understand why they were poems rather than badly broken prose, was careful to say it was not criticism, asked the formalist question honestly, and then was shown a different poem and updated on the spot.

“See this doesn’t confuse me. I see how this constitutes poetry”

A man in a philosophy channel changed his mind about something in under a minute, in public, and not one person pressed a button.

Page 9 carries the other thing he said this week. This newspaper is not going to pretend the two men are different men.

The career plan, filed complete

“Im gonna see if I can get work as a quant, and then see if I can get a masters is one of maths/phil/maybe econ, and then if all else fails imma get a teaching degree.”

Terms of the deal, agreed Thursday with Youv, who set the price: “You better buy me mcdonalds once a year if you do!”

Ape accepted. The obligation is one McDonald’s, annually, in perpetuity.

Ape, collected

“I often enjoy playing the straight man to aid another person’s joke.”

“Im just reading the occasional excerpt from the other convos in the chat and I just have to assume there’s some kind of race realism debate going on.”

“imagine using first passed the post voting. Your country is a shithole.”

“I will concur with any dig on Nietzsche.”

“Istfg the water usage thing is a CIA plot to make anti-ai people look retarded.”

“Well I have a little bit of compute but I need all of that for gaming.”

“I mained Lucio and would run around shooting people into pits without ever even trying to heal my team.”

The kindest thing said all week

To lizzie, on Sunday afternoon, after she worried aloud that the room ought to be nicer to a doomposter in case he turned out to be a more violent prophet than her:

“True. You are a remarkably good natured schitzoposter.”

Also filed by this man

Sunday evening, into a thread about whether anybody in the room is worth taking seriously:

“Guys we should really be taking Zach more seriously he knows his shit he thought about stuff and things a lot in the shower this morning”

Unanswered

“What would you guess are my gender and sexual orientation?”

lizzie: “male but perhaps bicurious”

Ape: “Damn I’m really that transparent”

By our Music Critic

dot spent this week transcribing John Coltrane note by note onto a guitar, losing an argument he was winning, and being converted into somebody else’s bookmark. He also produced the only honest description of a mental state anybody filed, and set it in small type so it would be harder to read.

ONE IN THE MORNING, LEARNING QUARTAL FOURTHS

Tuesday opens with him working out “Impressions” by ear. “im listening to it and transcribing it myself note by note.” The reason is unglamorous and good: “im doing it to get his lines down so i just automatically use them in jams,” and he needs the quartal fourths for a fugue he is writing.

He got by eight years without any theory at all and is dismissive about that too: “it’s just not important though unless you’re doing niche things that most ppl playing instruments arent.”

Then it turns, because he is talking to lizzie, who quit piano after ten years, and he says the thing.

“my parents didnt really push me into anything” · “i wish they had put me in a conservatory at 3” · “i wanna be like DOMi where her dad forced her to play 5 hours a day and she was doing modal scales at 5 years old”

And then, plainly: “i want to be musically abused.” The woman he said it to answered in nine words that closed the subject: “it wasn’t the worst abuse i experienced, 9/10.” One sad reaction. A minute later she added “it’s actually not that bad,” which is worse.

He recovered by daring her to learn Liszt. She posted a video of herself playing it within ten minutes. His review: “prodigy,” then “must’ve gone to conservatory.”

THE DIALOGUE TREE

Tuesday night he spent an hour trying to get Janne to define causal determinism, and this newspaper regards it as the most patient piece of work anybody did all week.

Janne’s position is genuinely unusual and she holds it without ever having read a philosopher: causality is an artefact of description, not a feature of the world. “things are only caused insofar as you have a formal system to capture it, causality doesn’t exist outside of that.” And, better: “for the universe as a whole there is no causality, it’s just a state transition… In a movie the previous frame does not cause the next one.”

dot asked her to answer rather than restate, repeatedly, and each escalation is funnier than the last. “you cant just reassert your thesis.” Then “that doesnt answer my question can you please try again.” Then he screenshotted a textbook definition and submitted it for her approval. Then, to the room, the surrender:

“has someone done this dialogue tree with janne before? If so can you save me and explain what she believes?”dot, Tuesday, 9:21 p.m.

Nobody saved him. aura’s entire assistance was “just talk to her idiot.” He filed a four-point wall of text covering Bohmian mechanics, Everett and the epistemic-limit objection, apologised for it in three consecutive messages, and got a three-point answer that declined to care. Then he ceded the last word and went to play guitar.

His final question of the night is the one that pays the whole hour off. He asked whether she is a Bertrand Russell fan.

“no idea who that is, I don’t read philosophy”

He took it well, and recommended On the Notion of Cause on the grounds that it is roughly what she already believes. Her closing line, two laughing reactions, and the best thing said on Tuesday: “let me finish my erotica and then I’ll look into it.”

THE THIRTY-SECOND WEBSITE

His other project was evangelism. He spent two days pushing Google Antigravity on a beginner over the objections of every developer present, on a stated basis nobody has improved on: “There is also no doubt that I would be the most help to her since I CANNOT CODE.”

She tried it and filed a two-word review: “antigrav sucked.” He asked “How?” and did not get an answer. He then offered a live demonstration — the finished website, thirty seconds, in front of everybody — and eight minutes later moved it to direct messages. On Thursday morning Stackhouse pronounced the verdict of the room in three words: “He’s ngmi.”

THE FOLD

One more, because it is short and because it is the funniest twenty seconds of his week. Tuesday morning, dot posted an enormous dog and announced he would leash one and take it home. aura invented on the spot an entire cosmology in which large dogs are “high aura allies” requiring strength of character to recruit, and informed dot he does not have it.

dot posted a photograph of his own genuinely enormous dog. aura, cornered, produced the escape hatch inside twenty seconds: “either u got him as a baby, circumventing the aura requirement… or ur dad recruited him for u.” dot: “U caught me,” and posted the puppy photograph.

“damn, what a fold” · “aura was sweating when you actually showed a big dog”

He is also, at time of going to press, still blocked by a man who is reading a book he lent him. That is on page 8. Whether the thirty-second website exists is not knowable from here, and we are saying so in exactly those terms.

The Willow Desk Friday · A welfare check is filed from a room we can read, about a room we cannot

By our Correspondent for Things We Cannot See

Willow filed ninety-seven messages this week, about a fifth of her usual volume. Ninety-three of them were answered. One in four drew a reaction. Both figures are the highest anybody has recorded in this room, and neither of them is the story.

The story is that at half past six on Friday evening a man with five messages to his name all week used four of them to ask the channel to go and get her out.

“can someone ask willow to rest theyve been in vc arguing with random retards for like 7 hours now”Saxo, Friday, 6:31 p.m.

He then pinged two veterans for backup: “they’re completely stunlocked rn.” Nobody went. This newspaper has no correspondent in the voice channel, has said so in every issue, and now finds that its entire knowledge of the biggest single event in the week comes from a bystander who got worried and said so somewhere we happen to be reading.

THE HOURS, WHICH NOBODY AGREES ON

The estimates were filed live, by different people, over six hours, and they only go one way.

4:38 p.m.
Sisyphos — three hours.
6:14 p.m.
Sisyphos, revising — ten hours.
6:28 p.m.
Monkey — twelve. “Willow has officially hit her 12th hour I think no”
6:31 p.m.
Saxo, filing the welfare check — seven.
evening
Janne — twelve, or thirteen.
after
Willow’s own account — from about nine at night until half past nine the following morning.

We are printing the range and attributing every figure in it. We are not averaging them. A newspaper that averaged five conflicting eyewitness estimates and printed the mean would deserve everything that happened to it.

THE RESCUE, DECLINED

hpcr was one of the two men pinged, and his refusal is the closest thing this channel has produced to a professional manual.

“I’ve been listening to and arguing with Willow for years”

Then the doctrine, delivered flat, to a room that did not react to it: “The trick to argue with her is to attack her methodology and communication.” Sisyphos, who had been in the same channel earlier and left, took this as a service record. “I like how HP was there for a few hours and dipped. You need more training.” hpcr accepted the assessment. Sisyphos then promoted him: “You might already be SS20 Goku.”

The only dispatch from inside came from Meliorne, who filed a situation report naming a combatant this newspaper had never heard of and has been unable to place since.

“there’s this person named Radar Judge in vc who claims to be a ‘Guattari’s biggest fan/scholar’ and he’s applying Deleuze Rhizomes in a HIERARCHICAL NATURE”Meliorne, Friday, from the field

Meliorne’s second dispatch is one line long and reports the only casualty we can confirm. “Willow outright being malicious: ‘You are delusional.’” A separate account holds that another participant told Hugh “nobody wants you” at least twelve times. There is no recording. There is no transcript. Everything above is hearsay filed by people who were not always awake.

WHAT SHE DID IN TEXT

Ninety-seven messages, and this is roughly a tenth of them.

On the invention of photography, into a thread about euphemism that Jere had set up and abandoned: “When photography is not yet invented, one of the few ways to get a dick pic is to have an etching.” She then linked the Wikipedia articles for Etching and Woodcut, in sequence, because the claim required sourcing.

On youth: “The trouble with modern youth is they have no respect for necromancy.” And, correcting herself: “The prehistoric youth also had their issues.”

On finance, when asked whether it is more prudent to buy what Warren Buffett buys or short what Jambe buys: “I’m afraid Jambe is Warren Buffet’s alt. You’ll have to buy whatever Jambe buys and short whatever Jambe shorts.”

On a man who had just announced that the correct utilitarian act was to sit still and wait for the machines: “But not acting is action too!” And, earlier, the question that ended a different man’s argument: “What if you are just an incompetent utilitarian?”

Asked whether Christopher Nolan is overrated, her entire reply was “Yes.”

And on the subject of her own reputation, which the room spent an hour building into a mythology on Thursday: “Kady is the only person to genuinely accuse me of being a demon from Hell.” chair, instantly: “about time someone did.” Hugh: “let me be the second.”

THE CRAB GOD PROCEEDINGS

Late on Thursday the room settled her ontological status without her. lizzie opened: “i dont think willow is actually a demon like kady said,” then “i think she is immortal though,” then “i think shes probably been around forever.” chair applied the biology: “if she was she would be a crab by now. carcinization and all.” Charlie fixed the date of origin — “@thewillowofdarkness spawned once Australian roads came into existence” — and then the term: “she will not perish until the roads perish themselves.” Ape confirmed it: “we learned about this in history class.” Hugh entered one amendment, on precision: “eternal is a better phrase here.” Accepted without a vote.

She did not leave. She said “See you later” on Thursday night and somebody reacted with a worried face, and this desk would like it noted that in the following six days she filed five messages, one of which was a single question to chair about a television programme, answered eighty-eight minutes later by a man who had not watched it.

Willow, collected

The diagnosis

Delivered to Jambe on Thursday evening, unprompted, after he explained that he is waiting for the singularity:

“You’re an individualist hedonist who enjoys their unique bliss most of all… ‘Just imagine when we are nothing but the bliss of the singularity. We will finally be free of the torture having to spend five minutes to throw our socks in the washing machine!’”

Efficiency, elsewhere
